idiom_name: envelope structure (header section + payload) owned by the integration layer, with a wrap/unwrap pair at each seam
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one envelope per wire contract - a header section (format indicator and version, correlation id, reply address, security metadata) plus an opaque payload - and place exactly two functions at each infrastructure seam: wrap(payload, metadata) and unwrap(envelope) -> (payload, metadata). Application code must only ever see the payload; the infrastructure must only ever see the envelope. Bind header names and encodings to a versioned, published schema, validate inbound header fields before trusting them, copy payload bytes instead of re-encoding when signatures must survive, and prefer the transport's own metadata channel (headers, properties, metadata) whenever it exists - wrapping inside the body is the fallback, not the default.
code_sketch:
wrap(payload, meta):
    env.headers = {version: 1, content_type: meta.type,
                   correlation_id: meta.cid, ...}
    env.body = payload              # bytes copied verbatim
    return encode(env)

unwrap(wire):
    env = decode(wire)
    verify(env.headers)             # validate before trusting
    return env.body                 # application sees the payload only
pitfalls: Wrapping in more than one place creates nested envelopes that every hop must peel; own the wrap/unwrap pair in the adapter, never in domain code.
A header field nobody validates is a spoofing surface (correlation ids, user ids, format indicators), especially when the infrastructure does not authenticate it.
Re-encoding the payload at every hop breaks signatures and digests and doubles the serialization cost.
